papers.title: How 'Real' is Your Real-Time Simultaneous Speech-to-Text Translation System?
papers.summary: Survey/critique arguing most SimulST research over-simplifies (pre-segmented speech, inconsistent terminology) and should adopt computation-aware latency, unbounded-speech evaluation, and SimulEval-based joint quality-latency curves.
key_findings: SimulEval is the dominant eval framework (61/110 papers surveyed)
computation-aware latency (incl. real compute time / RTF) is essential for honest benchmarking
cascade vs end-to-end: end-to-end trends better for simultaneous settings due to cascades accumulating ASR+MT delay and error propagation

papers.title: Re-Translation Strategies for Long Form, Simultaneous, Spoken Language Translation / Re-translation versus Streaming for Simultaneous Translation
papers.summary: Shows re-translation (re-translate the whole growing source on every ASR update) can match or beat streaming systems on final quality, but causes caption flicker; proposes masking (truncate last few words) and biasing (bias decoding toward the previous output) to nearly eliminate erasure while preserving quality.
key_findings: re-translation alone can be 'as good or better than SOTA streaming systems, even under constraints allowing very few revisions'
masking + biasing nearly eliminate erasure
directly describes this repo's current behavior: interim ASR results are re-translated (pipeline.py is_final=False path), i.e. re-translation without masking/biasing

papers.title: Turning Whisper into Real-Time Transcription System
papers.summary: LocalAgreement-n policy: only commit the longest common prefix agreed across n consecutive hypotheses from overlapping buffers. CUNI-KIT found n=2 most effective.
key_findings: LocalAgreement-2 is a simple, rule-based stability policy applicable to any incremental hypothesis stream, including our Deepgram interim-result -> LLM-translation stream

papers.title: Normalized erasure metric (definition)
papers.summary: Defines normalized erasure (NE): tokens deleted from the previous partial's suffix to produce the next partial (via longest common prefix), normalized by output length. NE=0 means no displayed token was ever revised.
key_findings: this repo currently logs chrF/latency/glossary but has zero instrumentation for revision/flicker -- direct, cheap, high-value gap to close first

papers.title: AlignAtt4LLM: Fast AlignAtt for Decoder-Only LLMs at IWSLT 2026 Simultaneous Speech Translation Task
papers.authors: unread -- found via WebSearch 2026-09-08, extracted via WebSearch 2026-09-08 (WebFetch blocked on arxiv.org in this environment, see note below)
papers.summary: A synchronous cascade for En->De/It/Zh: Qwen3-ASR with forced alignment produces an incrementally updated source transcript, and Gemma-4 E4B-it translates that prefix under an MT-side AlignAtt policy -- the first application of AlignAtt (attention-based emit-decision) to a decoder-only LLM, recovered despite the LLM lacking the encoder-decoder cross-attention earlier AlignAtt systems relied on, via (1) an explicit source span in the prompt, (2) offline-selected translation-specific alignment heads, (3) selective qk-fast replay of the draft-to-source attention block, and (4) runtime query/key capture that reproduces model outputs bit-identically. Outperforms IWSLT2026 baselines for En->De/It in both low-latency (~2s) and high-latency (<4s) regimes.
key_findings: AlignAtt's commit rule is fundamentally different from LocalAgreement-2: it inspects the LLM's own internal attention weights (which source tokens the next target token is attending to) to decide when enough of the source has been 'seen' to safely emit, not a longest-common-prefix agreement across repeated ASR hypotheses

Requires white-box access to the translating model's attention internals (offline alignment-head selection + runtime query/key capture) -- NOT reproducible against an API-only model like this repo's Gemini/OpenAI translator, where internal attention is inaccessible

Therefore this repo's h-localagreement-asr-commit should stay scoped to plain LocalAgreement-2 (agreement across consecutive Deepgram ASR hypotheses, both externally observable as text) rather than attempting an AlignAtt-style policy -- the reflections.md cycle-1 concern that AlignAtt4LLM's rule 'may differ from plain LocalAgreement-2 in a way that matters' is confirmed true, but the difference is a hard architectural blocker, not just a design nuance to account for

papers.title: Modeling and Improving Text Stability in Live Captions
papers.authors: Liu, Zhang, Du, et al. (Google Research)
papers.venue: ACM CHI 2023 (research.google blog post is a 2026-visible summary of the 2023 CHI paper, not a new 2026 paper)
papers.summary: Proposes a vision-based flicker metric -- luminance contrast + discrete Fourier transform applied to the *rendered* caption image, not a text/token diff -- to quantify what a viewer actually perceives as caption instability. Validated the metric against real viewer-reported distraction (moderate correlation, |r|~0.3) and introduced a stabilization algorithm (tokenized alignment + semantic merging + smooth animation) that a crowdsourced study (N=123) showed significantly reduces viewer distraction/fatigue and improves reading comfort.
key_findings: Vision-based (pixel/DFT) flicker measurement captures something text-based normalized erasure (NE) cannot: NE treats any token revision as equally bad, but a rendered-pixel metric would weight a revision by how visually jarring it actually is (position on screen, animation, font) -- NE is a reasonable cheap proxy but not a perceptual ground truth

The correlation with viewer experience is only moderate (~0.3), i.e. even a well-designed stability metric explains a minority of viewer-reported distraction -- a caution against over-indexing on any single flicker number (including this repo's own NE) as a proxy for caption quality

Out of scope for this repo right now: implementing this would require actually rendering captions to pixels and running DFT analysis, a much heavier lift than the retroactive text-level NE analysis already done in h-flicker-metric -- worth flagging as a possible future hypothesis (rendered-caption flicker) rather than pursuing this cycle

papers.title: NeMo@IWSLT 2026: Cascaded System for Simultaneous Speech Translation
papers.summary: NVIDIA's IWSLT 2026 submission cascades a dual-mode Unified ASR Transducer (trained to deliver stable transcriptions across a wide range of latencies) with a multilingual LLM for translation, covering En->De/It/Zh (standard and contextualized) and Cs->En. The key design choice is pushing stability into the ASR model itself via training, so the downstream LLM translation stage receives an already-stable source stream instead of needing its own stabilization logic.
key_findings: Confirms stability is being treated as a first-class training/architecture concern by 2026 SOTA cascade systems, not just a post-hoc metric -- validates this repo's decision (h-flicker-metric) to start measuring it at all

NeMo's approach (train the ASR model itself for cross-latency stability) is not retrofittable to this repo, which uses Deepgram as an off-the-shelf hosted ASR API with no training access -- this repo's realistic options remain post-hoc: masking (h-masking-holdback) or commit-gating (h-localagreement-asr-commit) applied to Deepgram's existing interim/final hypothesis stream

WebSearch could not surface NeMo's specific stability metric formula or numeric results (only the architecture-level design rationale) -- the full ACL Anthology paper (WebFetch to aclanthology.org is blocked in this environment, see note below) would be needed for a numeric comparison; not blocking any current hypothesis since NeMo's approach isn't applicable here anyway

papers.title: Improving Stability in Simultaneous Speech Translation: A Revision-Controllable Decoding Approach
papers.summary: Introduces an 'allowed revision window' into the beam-search pruning step of a streaming translation decoder: candidate continuations whose new output would revise more than a bounded number of previously-emitted tokens are pruned out during beam search itself, rather than emitted and corrected later. Because the constraint sits inside decoding (not as a post-hoc mask/filter on top of an unconstrained re-translation), the revision window can be tuned continuously from 0 (completely eliminates flicker) to unbounded (behaves like ordinary unconstrained re-translation), letting a system pick any point on the stability/quality tradeoff curve rather than only two fixed regimes.
key_findings: Revision budget is enforced during beam search/pruning, not as a separate masking step applied after generation -- structurally different from Arivazhagan et al. 2020's masking (truncate last k words of already-generated output) and biasing (soft preference for previous output), which post-process an unconstrained re-translation

The window size is a single continuous knob: window=0 gives zero flicker (nothing already shown is ever revised), and results show quality degrades only modestly as the window shrinks toward 0, i.e. most of the achievable quality is retained even under a tight/no-revision budget

NOT directly applicable to this repo without white-box decoder access: this repo's translator is an API-only LLM (Gemini/OpenAI) where beam-search pruning internals are not exposed by the API, so the revision-window mechanism itself can't be implemented -- but the *result* (a continuous stability/quality tradeoff curve exists and near-zero-flicker costs little quality) is useful evidence that this repo's own masking-based approach (h-masking-holdback) is a reasonable API-accessible approximation of the same idea, and suggests reporting a similar quality-vs-mask-window curve rather than a single on/off comparison

papers.title: Self-Speculative Biased Decoding for Faster Re-Translation
papers.authors: Linxiao Zeng, Haoyun Deng, Kangyuan Shu, Shizhen Wang (Zoom Communications)
papers.summary: Targets the *compute cost* of re-translation (not directly flicker): re-translating the whole growing source on every ASR update is redundant because most of the new output matches the previous output. Self-Speculative Biased Decoding (SSBD) reuses the model's own previous output as a speculative draft for the updated (longer) input, verifies the whole draft in one forward pass with a lightweight bias term, and only resumes normal autoregressive decoding from the first token where the draft and the verified continuation diverge -- a tuning-free inference-time trick, no fine-tuning required. Separately, it introduces a 'display-only masking' UI trick: hide the unstable tail of the output from the viewer while still keeping it internally as the speculative draft for the next round's verification.
key_findings: Directly names and formalizes exactly the caption-visible-vs-internally-fluid distinction that this repo's h-gemini-only-masking-replay hypothesis is built on ('display-only masking' = show only the stable prefix, keep computing/holding the unstable suffix) -- this is now real published grounding for that hypothesis's core mechanism, not just an informal design choice

The speculative-decoding speedup mechanism itself (verify-then-resume-from-divergence) targets LLM inference cost/latency, which this repo doesn't control at the API level (Gemini/OpenAI are called as black-box completion endpoints, no access to draft/verify at the token level) -- not implementable here, but its stated motivation (repeated full re-translation is wasteful because most output is unchanged) is exactly the same waste this repo's re-translate-every-interim-update pipeline.py path exhibits

'Tuning-free' and applied at inference time on an off-the-shelf LLM (not a custom-trained model) -- same deployment constraint as this repo (Gemini/OpenAI, not self-hosted), reinforcing that this is the most relevant of the 4 new papers found this cycle for this repo's actual architecture

papers.title: Hierarchical Policy Optimization for Simultaneous Translation of Unbounded Speech
papers.authors: Siqi Ouyang, Shuoyang Ding, Oleksii Hrinchuk, Vitaly Lavrukhin, Brian Yan, Boris Ginsburg, Lei Li (CMU + NVIDIA)
papers.summary: Builds on prior work that reformulates simultaneous speech translation as a multi-turn dialogue task so the LLM's KV-cache can be reused across turns instead of recomputing from scratch on every input growth (directly the same 'full re-translation every update is wasteful' problem SSBD above addresses, but solved via training instead of inference-time tricks). That prior multi-turn-SFT approach needs dialogue-form training data that's scarce and hard to synthesize well. This paper's contribution is Hierarchical Policy Optimization (HPO), an RL post-training step on top of imperfect SFT data, using a hierarchical reward balancing translation quality against latency. Reports En->Zh/De/Ja results: +7 COMET and +1.25 MetricX over the SFT-only baseline at a fixed 1.5s latency budget.
key_findings: Explicitly evaluates En->Japanese (this repo's exact language pair) and reports it improves substantially with RL post-training over a naive multi-turn SFT baseline -- concrete evidence that multi-turn/KV-cache-reuse framing for streaming translation continuations works for En->Ja specifically, not just European-language pairs

Entirely a training-time method (RL fine-tuning of an open-weights model with accessible KV-cache) -- NOT applicable to this repo, which calls Gemini/OpenAI as closed API endpoints with no fine-tuning or KV-cache access exposed for this use case

Useful negative/contextual finding for h-cross-utterance-flicker: this paper's whole premise (treat each new utterance/continuation as a new turn reusing cached context, rather than as an independent from-scratch re-translation) is precisely the training-time fix for the cross-batch 'near-total rewrite' problem this repo measured empirically in cycle 4 (cross-batch translation NE ~1.47). Confirms the cross-batch drift this repo found is a recognized, actively-researched problem in 2026 SOTA systems, but the SOTA fix requires model access this repo doesn't have -- reinforces that any fix here must be prompt-engineering-level (e.g. explicitly passing prior-utterance translation as context in the prompt) rather than architectural

papers.title: DOA: Training-Free Decoder-Only Attention Policy for Long-Form Simultaneous Translation with SpeechLLMs
papers.authors: Sara Papi, Luisa Bentivogli (Fondazione Bruno Kessler)
papers.summary: Addresses the same READ/WRITE emit-timing problem as AlignAtt(4LLM), but for decoder-only Speech-LLMs that (unlike encoder-decoder AlignAtt systems) have no explicit cross-attention between source audio and generated text to read an alignment signal from. DOA derives a proxy alignment purely from the decoder's own self-attention weights (attention from generated text tokens back onto the audio/prompt tokens in the shared decoder stream), training-free, and uses it as the emit-decision policy for long-form (not just single-utterance) simultaneous translation.
key_findings: Same family as AlignAtt4LLM (already read, cycle 2): both need white-box access to the translating model's attention weights at inference time (offline-selected alignment heads for AlignAtt4LLM, self-attention proxy for DOA) -- neither is implementable against this repo's API-only Gemini/OpenAI translator, which exposes no attention weights

'Training-free' here means no fine-tuning of the SpeechLLM is needed, not that it works with a black-box API -- it still requires the caller to run the model locally and read internal activations, which this repo's API-based architecture structurally cannot do

Reconfirms (a second time, independently of AlignAtt4LLM) that attention-based emit policies are the dominant 2026 research direction for LLM-based SimulST, but also reconfirms this repo's earlier decision to scope h-localagreement-asr-commit to plain LocalAgreement-2 (observable-text-only) is the right call given the API-only constraint -- no new action needed, just additional grounding for a decision already made

papers.title: Dynamic Lagging for Simultaneous Translation
papers.summary: Microsoft Research paper on cascaded SimulST addressing exactly the flicker problem this repo measured in h-cross-utterance-flicker (cross-batch translation NE~1.47). Fine-tunes a sentence-trained decoder-only LLM (Qwen3-8B) to be 'prefix-aware' by training it on stable prefixes -- the longest prefix any partial-source translation shares with the model's own full-source translation -- mixed with ordinary full-sentence pairs. At inference, the model is prompted with a single force-decode turn that carries the previously committed target text forward as more source arrives, so the output is flicker-free by construction rather than by post-hoc masking. Evaluated EN->DE/JA/ZH with simulated streaming via reference-transcript prefixes.
key_findings: Directly targets this repo's own confirmed problem (cross-batch translation NE~1.47 vs ~0.0001 within-batch, from h-cross-utterance-flicker) with a named mechanism: commit-forward via force-decoding the previously emitted target as a prefix.
The core method requires fine-tuning (LoRA/full on Qwen3-8B) which this repo's API-only Gemini/OpenAI translator cannot do -- not directly implementable as-is.

However the *inference-time shape* of the fix (force-decode/carry-forward the previously committed translation as context for the next continuation batch) is a prompt-level idea achievable without fine-tuning: pass the prior batch's emitted Japanese text back into the prompt for the next batch and instruct the model to extend/preserve it rather than re-translating from scratch -- this is a plausible zero-shot approximation worth testing as a new hypothesis.
EN->JA is one of the three evaluated language pairs, so this is directly on-target for the repo's EN->JA use case rather than a different-language-pair result that may not transfer.

papers.title: MLLP-VRAIN UPV system for the IWSLT 2026 Simultaneous Speech Translation task
papers.summary: UPV/MLLP-VRAIN's IWSLT 2026 SimulST shared-task system report. Builds a cascaded pipeline (Parakeet ASR + Qwen 3.5 MT) with adaptive 'black-box' read/write policies -- i.e. policies that only need the model's observable output, not internal attention weights, distinguishing it from the AlignAtt-family papers already read (alignatt4llm-iwslt2026, papi2026-doa) that need white-box access this repo's API-only translator doesn't have. Also describes allowing the last two previously emitted target tokens to be rewritten when a 'catastrophic failure' is detected, keeping the resulting flicker minimal. For three of the En-> language directions they also add a context track: ASR word-boosting plus a RAG mechanism over offline pre-translated exemplars for domain-specific context.
key_findings: Black-box policy framing (no internal model access needed) is architecturally compatible with this repo's API-only Gemini/OpenAI translator, unlike the AlignAtt/DOA family already read -- worth another look for the emit-timing hypothesis (h-localagreement-asr-commit) as an alternative or complement to plain LocalAgreement-2.

The 'rewrite only the last two tokens unless catastrophic failure' idea is conceptually the same shape as this repo's existing h-masking-holdback hypothesis (bound how much of a re-translation is allowed to change) but framed as a *decoding-time* constraint rather than a masking/prompt constraint -- could sharpen h-masking-holdback's design (e.g., cap edit distance between successive translation_partial revisions instead of/in addition to masking source text).

The RAG-over-pre-translated-exemplars context track is for domain adaptation (glossary-like), overlapping conceptually with this repo's existing keyterm/glossary features already tested in prior experiments -- not a new angle by itself.

No fully aligned latency/quality numbers surfaced via WebSearch snippets alone (WebFetch to arxiv.org is EGRESS_BLOCKED in this sandbox, consistent with cycles 2-5); the MCIF En->De +5.82 XCOMET-XL year-over-year figure found is for a different track/direction than this repo's En->Ja and not directly comparable.

papers.title: LLMs Are Zero-Shot Context-Aware Simultaneous Translators
papers.authors: Roman Koshkin, Katsuhito Sudoh, Satoshi Nakamura (NAIST)
papers.summary: NAIST group's EMNLP 2024 paper (toLLMatch) showing that open-source LLMs, used zero-shot with no fine-tuning, can match or beat prior specialized SimulST baselines by exploiting document/discourse-level context passed in the prompt. This is architecturally the closest match found so far to this repo's own setup: an API/prompt-level LLM translator with no access to model internals or weights. They report that injecting even minimal background/context information into the prompt gives further gains, especially on technical/domain-specific subject matter.
key_findings: Zero-shot, prompt-only context injection (no fine-tuning) is directly reproducible against this repo's Gemini-API-based translator -- the most 'free lunch' shaped finding of any paper read so far, since it needs no architecture change, just prompt content.

'Injecting minimal background information' for gains on technical subject matter overlaps with this repo's existing keyterm/glossary/domain features (already tested), but the paper's specific mechanism is discourse-level context (e.g. prior sentences/utterances), not a static glossary -- this is the same shape of idea as passing the previously-committed translation of an utterance's earlier batches forward as prompt context, which is exactly what h-cross-utterance-flicker's finding (cross-batch NE~1.47) suggests this repo is currently NOT doing.

Reference open-source implementation exists (github.com/RomanKoshkin/toLLMatch) that could be read for the exact prompt template/context-window mechanics if this becomes a hypothesis, though re-implementing against this repo's own Gemini-based pipeline (not toLLMatch's specific backbone) would still be needed.

Combined with hoang2026-dynamic-lagging's force-decode/commit-forward idea, this strongly suggests a concrete, zero-cost-to-implement (prompt-only, no fine-tuning) new hypothesis: pass each utterance's already-committed/most-stable prior translation text back into the prompt for its next continuation batch, instructing the model to extend rather than re-translate from scratch, then re-measure cross-batch translation NE the same way h-cross-utterance-flicker did.

papers.title: Better late than never: Meta-evaluation of latency metrics for simultaneous speech-to-text translation
papers.summary: First large-scale meta-evaluation of latency metrics for simultaneous speech-to-text translation, comparing metrics against a defined "True Latency" ground truth across languages and systems. Finds existing latency metrics are inconsistent and structurally biased by how the reference audio is segmented into sentences/utterances. Introduces YAAL (Yet Another Average Lagging) plus SOFTSEGMENTER, a segmentation-aware evaluation suite for both short- and long-form simultaneous translation.
key_findings: Segmentation bias is structural: metrics disagree more when reference segmentation changes, not just when system quality changes.
YAAL reaches 98% pairwise system-ranking accuracy vs True Latency ground truth, vs 54-73% for established metrics on degenerate/edge-case systems.
SOFTSEGMENTER is proposed as a segmentation-robust companion tool for long-form audio, where utterance boundaries are ambiguous.
Directly relevant to this repo's own flicker/latency metrics (flicker_metrics.py) as a check on whether our latency numbers could be segmentation-sensitive in the same way.

papers.title: Simultaneous Translation with Offline Speech and LLM Models in CUNI Submission to IWSLT 2025
papers.summary: CUNI's IWSLT 2025 submission using offline (non-streaming) speech and LLM models for simultaneous translation, selected via COMET-XL and evaluated with LongYAAL latency metrics. Section 5.1 introduces a character-level "Continuous Levenshtein Alignment" (CLA) method for measuring ASR word latency, with an open-source implementation (github.com/ufal/asr_latency).
key_findings: CLA aligns gold and ASR-candidate transcripts at the character level (not word level), which is more robust to minor deviations like word-ending mismatches.

The alignment algorithm prefers continuous runs of copy/substitute edits over interruptions from inserts/deletes, avoiding "coincident alignment" to a deleted/inserted token that would produce an unrealistic latency value.

Crucially, this is a RETROACTIVE metric: it runs on existing timestamped gold transcripts + ASR candidate outputs after the fact, with no live/streaming ASR access needed -- confirmed via the repo README (processes ~11 min of transcript in ~1 min).

This directly matches the "evaluation methodology that does not need live ASR" gap from cycle 8 REFLECT, and could in principle be run against this repo's existing experiments/*.json asr_interim timestamps without any new API spend.

papers.title: BeaverTalk: Oregon State University's IWSLT 2025 Simultaneous Speech Translation System
papers.summary: Oregon State University's IWSLT 2025 cascaded system: VAD segmenter -> Whisper Large V2 ASR -> Gemma 3 12B (LoRA fine-tuned) for translation. Uses a conversational prompting strategy that carries a single prior-sentence memory bank from the source language into the prompt for the next sentence, to keep translations consistent across sentence boundaries in a streaming context.
key_findings: Memory bank is deliberately small: ONE prior source-language sentence, not the full running transcript -- a concrete, minimal design point for what "context anchor" should carry.

Reports En->De BLEU 24.64/27.83 and En->Zh BLEU 34.07/37.23 at StreamLAAL 1837.86/3343.73 and 2216.99/3521.35 respectively (low/high latency regimes) -- gives a rough BLEU-vs-latency operating point for a memory-bank-style system, usable as an external sanity check even though metrics/domain differ from this repo's chrF-based ones.

The prior sentence used as context is the SOURCE-language sentence, not the target-language translation -- worth flagging as a design choice to consider for h-continuation-context-anchor, which should specify explicitly whether it anchors on source or target text.

Uses a fine-tuned (LoRA) LLM rather than a frozen general-purpose LLM via prompting alone -- a caveat when using this as grounding for a prompting-only (no fine-tuning) hypothesis like h-continuation-context-anchor in this repo, since gains may partly come from the fine-tuning rather than the memory-bank prompting alone.

papers.title: ExPosST: Explicit Positioning with Adaptive Masking for LLM-Based Simultaneous Machine Translation
papers.authors: Xiamen University, Xiaomi Inc., University of Hong Kong -- extracted via WebSearch 2026-09-13 (WebFetch blocked on arxiv.org in this environment)
papers.summary: ExPosST targets a specific engineering problem in applying decoder-only LLMs to simultaneous MT: as source tokens arrive incrementally and the prompt is naively re-sent/re-tokenized, target-token positions shift on every update, forcing implementations to choose between reusing the KV cache (fast, but positionally inconsistent with training) or recomputing from scratch each time (positionally correct, but slow). It fixes this with (1) pre-allocated positional slots for incoming source tokens so target positions never move regardless of how much source has arrived yet, letting the KV cache be reused safely, and (2) policy-consistent fine-tuning that trains the model under the same incremental-decoding behavior it will see at inference time. It is a decoding/serving-layer technique for a self-hosted, fine-tunable LLM -- not a prompting trick applicable to an API-only model.
key_findings: The positional-mismatch problem ExPosST solves is specific to decoder-only LLMs that get re-prompted with a growing source prefix at inference time -- this repo's pipeline instead re-sends the full accumulated source text as a fresh prompt each translation call (per _stream_batch()'s docstring, confirmed by h-cross-utterance-flicker's finding that continuation batches aren't append-only), so there is no persistent KV cache being reused across calls in the first place; ExPosST's KV-cache-preservation benefit doesn't apply to this architecture as-is.

Requires fine-tuning access to the model's own weights (policy-consistent fine-tuning) -- not compatible with this repo's API-only Gemini/OpenAI usage, similar to the earlier finding for alignatt4llm-iwslt2026's white-box attention requirement.

Relevant only if this repo ever moves to a self-hosted/fine-tunable translation model; not actionable against the current API-based architecture. Keep h-masking-holdback and h-localagreement-asr-commit scoped to what they already are (text-level, prompt-side interventions) rather than trying to adapt ExPosST's decoding-layer approach.

papers.title: Simultaneous Masking, Not Prompting Optimization: A Paradigm Shift in Fine-tuning LLMs for Simultaneous Translation
papers.authors: unread -- extracted via WebSearch 2026-09-13 (WebFetch blocked on arxiv.org in this environment)
papers.summary: SimulMask reframes how you fine-tune an LLM for simultaneous translation: instead of teaching a decision policy (e.g. wait-k) through data augmentation or prompt engineering (which bloats training data, wastes compute rebuilding the KV cache as prompts grow, and locks the model to one policy), it bakes the policy directly into training-time attention masks, so the model learns to translate under the same masking pattern it will face online. Reported to match or beat prompting-based fine-tuning on translation quality while being cheaper to train, across multiple language pairs and latency settings (EMNLP 2024; exact chrF/BLEU numbers weren't recoverable from search snippets since arxiv.org WebFetch is blocked in this environment).
key_findings: Like ExPosST, this is a fine-tuning-time technique -- it requires training/adapting model weights under a masking regime, which this repo's API-only LLM usage (Gemini/OpenAI, no fine-tuning access) cannot replicate.

The conceptual link to this repo's h-masking-holdback is only superficial: SimulMask's 'masking' is an attention mask applied during LLM training to teach a decision policy, whereas h-masking-holdback's 'masking' is truncating the last N words of the ASR text before it's ever sent to the LLM, at inference time, with no fine-tuning involved. Same word, unrelated mechanisms -- do not conflate the two in future hypotheses.

No actionable follow-up for this repo given the API-only constraint; noting the distinction is itself the useful outcome of this read, so a future cycle doesn't waste a hypothesis slot chasing an inapplicable idea just because both papers use the word 'masking'.

papers.title: Best Speech-to-Text Providers 2026: Independent Benchmarks & How to Choose
papers.venue: Coval.ai blog (independent vendor benchmark, not peer-reviewed)
papers.summary: Independent 2026 benchmark comparing 5 streaming STT vendors (Gradium STT, Deepgram Nova-2, Deepgram Nova-3, AssemblyAI Universal Streaming, ElevenLabs Scribe v2) on time-to-first-token latency and word error rate, 2,400 runs per model. Finds a real speed/accuracy tradeoff across current vendors: the fastest two (Deepgram Nova-2/Nova-3, ~992ms median TTFT) also have the highest WER in the comparison (25.2-25.3%), while the most accurate (Gradium STT, 2.4% WER) is slower. Also flags Deepgram Flux Multilingual (released 2026-04-29, after this repo's Deepgram model choice was made) as the first conversational STT with built-in end-of-turn detection, claiming under 300ms median EOT and a 200-600ms saving over a separate STT+VAD pipeline.
key_findings: This repo already uses Deepgram Nova-3 (per experiments/results.csv's deepgram_model column) -- the benchmark's ~25% WER figure for Nova-3 is a general voice-agent-domain number, not specific to this repo's ml_transformers/en_talk domains, so should be treated as an outside data point corroborating that ASR error is a real cost of choosing Deepgram for speed, not as a number to plug directly into this repo's own WER tracking.

The Flux Multilingual end-of-turn-detection feature is the concrete new lead: h-endpointing-connection-verify already confirmed (2026-09-12, static code audit) that this repo's deepgram_endpointing config value does reach Deepgram's connection params correctly, but that hypothesis's own flagged open question (whether flat asr_word_latency_cla_mean_s across the whole endpointing sweep is because the clip doesn't exercise the threshold, vs. some other reason) is unresolved -- Flux's built-in EOT detection would replace this repo's manual endpointing/utterance_end_ms tuning entirely rather than just adjusting it, which is a bigger question than what h-endpointing-connection-verify was scoped to answer.

Independent vendor blog, not peer-reviewed, and WebFetch on coval.ai is blocked in this environment so these numbers are WebSearch-snippet-only -- treat as a lead to verify (e.g. by reading the Deepgram Flux announcement directly) before proposing any migration, not as a citable number for the Japanese report.

papers.title: SimulU: Training-free Policy for Long-form Simultaneous Speech-to-Speech Translation
papers.summary: SimulU proposes a training-free simultaneous speech-to-speech translation policy that reuses the cross-attention weights already present inside pretrained end-to-end S2ST models to decide both how much prior context to keep and when to emit output, avoiding the extra training most prior SimulST policies require. It specifically targets long-form, non-pre-segmented audio -- the same unbounded-speech evaluation gap papi2025-howreal already flagged -- and reports a comparable-or-better quality-latency trade-off vs. strong cascaded baselines on MuST-C across 8 languages, though exact figures weren't recoverable via WebSearch snippets in this sandbox (arxiv.org/huggingface.co fetches were EGRESS_BLOCKED). Its core idea -- deriving history/commit decisions from attention signal already inside the model, rather than heuristics -- is the same territory as h-localagreement-asr-commit, but doesn't transfer directly here since this repo's target LLM (Gemini/GPT) is an opaque API with no accessible cross-attention; useful only as a conceptual contrast, not an implementable technique.
key_findings: First training-free policy for long-form (not pre-segmented) simultaneous speech-to-speech translation.

Exploits cross-attention weights already present in pretrained end-to-end S2ST models to drive two decisions: (1) history management -- how much prior input/output context to keep -- and (2) speech-output selection -- when to commit/emit output -- without any additional training.

Motivation: most prior SimulST/S2ST policies require resource-intensive training and are evaluated on short, pre-segmented utterances, so they don't generalize to continuous (long-form) speech -- the same unbounded-speech gap papi2025-howreal already flagged for this corpus.
Evaluated on MuST-C across 8 languages; reports a better-or-comparable quality-latency trade-off vs. strong cascaded baselines.

No numeric quality/latency figures surfaced via WebSearch snippets (WebFetch to arxiv.org/huggingface.co both EGRESS_BLOCKED in this sandbox, consistent with the cycle-2/cycle-9 notes below) -- treat as directionally useful, not a precise benchmark to cite numbers from.

papers.title: Do LLMs Need Architectural Changes for Simultaneous Speech Translation? A Prefix-to-Prefix Data Driven Approach
papers.authors: Chen, Xue, Tang, Heba, Gholami, Fan, Li
papers.summary: This paper asks whether decoder-only LLM-based SimulST needs architectural changes to stream well and answers no: fine-tuning a chunked streaming speech-encoder-LLM on teacher-labeled prefix-to-prefix targets with a rewind-capable committed prefix (CSSEL-P2P) closes most of the gap to non-streaming quality with no architecture change, improving +1.54 COMETKiwi over the streaming baseline at only +0.15s more Average Lagging. The lesson is that the win comes from training-time supervision on committed/retractable prefixes, not from prompting or inference-time heuristics. This bears directly on h-localagreement-asr-commit's inference-time-only (prompting/masking) approach: if this repo's prompting-only masking shows a smaller effect than this paper's fine-tuned approach, that is consistent with -- not contradicted by -- this paper's finding, since this repo does not fine-tune anything.
key_findings: Asks whether decoder-only LLM SimulST needs architectural changes at all, and answers with a purely data-driven alternative: no.

Method (CSSEL-P2P): fixed-length audio chunks fed to a chunked streaming speech-encoder-LLM (CSSEL) doing cumulative streaming decoding with a rewind-based committed prefix (i.e. a commit policy that can retract/rewrite its own tail, not append-only), fine-tuned on teacher-labeled prefix-to-prefix (P2P) targets with bounded waiting.

Result (in-house conversational speech eval): CSSEL-P2P improves streaming quality by +1.54 COMETKiwi over the CSSEL streaming baseline at comparable latency (+0.15s Average Lagging) -- i.e. supervision/data design closed most of the gap to non-streaming quality without touching model architecture.

Relevance to this repo: directly on-point for h-localagreement-asr-commit's territory -- this repo's LocalAgreement/masking hypotheses are an inference-time-only analogue of the same 'commit-with-revision' idea, and this paper's rewind-based committed prefix is a training-based version of what this repo tries to approximate via prompting/masking alone. Useful contrast for result_summary framing: if this repo's prompting-only approach underperforms, that's consistent with this paper's finding that fine-tuned supervision (not prompting) is what actually buys the quality-latency win.

papers.title: The Trade-off Was in the Labels: Causal Supervision for Turn-Aware Streaming ASR
papers.summary: This paper argues silence-duration-only endpointing is fundamentally the wrong signal for turn detection, since within-turn pauses in natural speech routinely exceed between-turn gaps -- what actually distinguishes a turn boundary is whether the words spoken so far form a semantically complete thought. It introduces a small LoRA adapter fine-tuned on Qwen3-ASR-0.6B (trainable in hours on one GPU) that jointly transcribes and detects end-of-turn from meaning plus silence, reporting 0.97 boundary recall at 0.39s median latency with only 0.3 false end-of-turn fires per speech-minute on a deployment-matched benchmark. For this repo it is a concrete, small-footprint, self-hostable alternative to Deepgram's built-in silence-based endpointing, and a candidate explanation for any flicker/latency issues that persist regardless of vendor, since it argues the ceiling is inherent to silence-only endpointing rather than vendor-specific.
key_findings: Core claim: within-turn pauses routinely exceed between-turn gaps in natural speech, so silence-duration-only endpointing (what this repo's Deepgram integration currently relies on) is fundamentally the wrong signal -- what actually distinguishes a turn boundary is whether the words spoken so far form a semantically complete thought.

Method: a small LoRA adapter fine-tuned on Qwen3-ASR-0.6B (trained in hours on one GPU) that jointly transcribes, detects end-of-turn from meaning + silence (not silence alone), handles dictation, and grounds transcription in context. First open training recipe + benchmark for turn-aware streaming ASR.
Reported numbers (deployment-matched benchmark, replicated on a fresh test set): 0.97 boundary recall at 0.39s median latency, with 0.3 false end-of-turn fires per speech-minute.

Code/recipe/benchmark released on GitHub (per WebSearch snippet; exact repo URL not confirmed -- WebFetch to arxiv.org/github.com not attempted this cycle beyond the blocked arxiv.org fetch, follow up if this becomes a live hypothesis).

Relevance to this repo: directly grounds h-endpointing-connection-verify -- this is a concrete, small-footprint (single LoRA, single GPU-hours) alternative to Deepgram's built-in endpointing that this repo could in principle self-host once/if the Deepgram websocket path is confirmed reachable; also a candidate explanation if endpointing-related flicker/latency issues persist even after the Deepgram connectivity question is resolved, since it argues silence-based endpointing has an inherent ceiling regardless of vendor.

papers.title: Redefining Machine Simultaneous Interpretation: From Incremental Translation to Human-Like Strategies
papers.venue: ACL 2026 Findings (also arXiv:2509.21801 / listed here as 2601.11002)
papers.summary: Argues that a binary READ/WRITE policy caps SiMT quality-latency tradeoffs because it cannot restructure content the way human interpreters do. Adds four adaptive actions (SENTENCE_CUT, DROP, PARTIAL_SUMMARIZATION, PRONOMINALIZATION) to a decoder-only LLM SiMT framework, trained with action-aware prompting so the model learns *when* to cut, drop, summarize or pronominalize as well as what to say. Evaluated with a custom latency-aware TTS pipeline (renders text output to speech with realistic timing) rather than token-count-only latency proxies. On ACL60/60 En-Zh/En-De it beats salami (fixed-chunk) baselines on both COMET-KIWI and delay.
key_findings: READ/WRITE-only SiMT policies are structurally limited; human interpreters routinely restructure, omit, and simplify, which a binary policy cannot express.
PARTIAL_SUMMARIZATION and DROP actions are the two actions doing most of the latency-improving work in their ablations (per the abstract framing).
Evaluating simultaneous MT quality/latency via a TTS-rendered speech proxy, not just text token timestamps, is presented as more representative of real interpreter-style delay.

Directly relevant to this repo: our LLM translation prompt currently only ever emits a literal translation per ASR segment/utterance -- no analogous "drop this filler" or "summarize this ASR run-on" action exists in llm_translator.py's SYSTEM_PROMPT_TEMPLATE (verified: its numbered rules cover target-only translation, continuation flow, terminology preservation, and the uncertain-marker convention -- nothing about compressing or dropping content), which could be a source of unnecessary output length/latency on long, disfluent utterances.
papers.extracted_abstract: SiMT with only READ/WRITE actions cannot fully address quality-latency tradeoffs. Proposes 4 new adaptive actions for a decoder-only LLM SiMT framework: SENTENCE_CUT, DROP, PARTIAL_SUMMARIZATION, PRONOMINALIZATION, enabling real-time restructuring, omission, and simplification while preserving semantic fidelity. Training references built via action-aware prompting. Built a latency-aware TTS pipeline to map textual outputs to speech with realistic timing for evaluation. On ACL60/60 En-Zh and En-De, consistently improves COMET-KIWI and achieves lower delay vs. reference translations and salami (fixed-latency chunk) baselines.

papers.title: Streaming Translation and Transcription Through Speech-to-Text Causal Alignment
papers.summary: Proposes Hikari, a fully end-to-end streaming ST+transcription model that replaces hand-built or learned READ/WRITE policies with a probabilistic WAIT token baked directly into decoding, so the policy is learned jointly with translation rather than bolted on. Adds "Decoder Time Dilation" to cut autoregressive-decoding overhead and balance the training distribution between WAIT and emit steps, plus supervised fine-tuning specifically for recovering from delay (i.e. catching back up after the model has fallen behind). Reports new SOTA BLEU on En->Ja/De/Ru across both low- and high-latency operating points.
key_findings: A learned, policy-free WAIT-token mechanism integrated into decoding is proposed as a replacement for external READ/WRITE heuristics (e.g. our own LocalAgreement-2/masking-holdback approach, which is exactly this kind of external heuristic).

Explicit "recover from delay" fine-tuning is called out as materially improving the quality-latency trade-off -- i.e. training for the case where the model/pipeline has fallen behind real-time, not just the steady-state case.
En->Ja is one of the three evaluated language pairs, directly matching this repo's target direction.

This is an end-to-end trained-model approach (not applicable to our cascade of Deepgram ASR + prompted LLM translation without retraining a model) -- relevant as a conceptual benchmark/ceiling reference, not as a directly implementable change here.
papers.extracted_abstract: Proposes Hikari, a policy-free, fully end-to-end model for simultaneous speech-to-text translation + streaming transcription, replacing hand-engineered/learned READ-WRITE policies with a probabilistic WAIT token mechanism baked into decoding. Introduces "Decoder Time Dilation" to reduce autoregressive overhead and balance the training distribution, plus an SFT strategy that trains the model to recover from delays, improving the quality-latency trade-off. Evaluated En->Ja/De/Ru; reports new SOTA BLEU in both low- and high-latency regimes vs recent baselines.

papers.title: Streaming Speech-to-Text Translation with a SpeechLLM
papers.authors: Titouan Parcollet, Shucong Zhang, Xianrui Zheng, Rogier C. van Dalen (Samsung AI Center, Cambridge)
papers.summary: Points out that most "SpeechLLM" speech translation systems are not actually streaming: they wait for a full utterance or emit at fixed intervals. Proposes training the LLM to jointly decide (a) what to emit and (b) whether it has already seen enough audio to emit it yet, using automatic input-speech/output-text alignments as training signal rather than a hand-designed policy. Across language pairs, reaches quality close to a non-streaming baseline at only 1-2s latency.
key_findings: Frames "wait for a full utterance" and "emit at fixed intervals" as the two common streaming anti-patterns -- notably, our own pipeline's Deepgram-endpointing-triggered translation trigger is architecturally closer to the first anti-pattern (wait for utterance-end) than to a token-level incremental policy.

Automatic speech/text alignment is used as training supervision for the emit-timing decision, an end-to-end-training-only technique not directly portable to a prompted, non-finetuned LLM setup like this repo's.

1-2s latency at near-non-streaming quality is a concrete target number worth citing in future latency-budget discussions for this repo, even though the achieving mechanism (joint emit-timing training) is not reusable here without model training infrastructure.

Reinforces (independently of the Hikari paper above) that the current research direction in the field is moving policy decisions inside the model via training, away from external heuristics like ours -- useful context for why our LocalAgreement-2/masking-holdback experiments (h-localagreement-asr-commit, h-masking-holdback) are already near the ceiling of what a heuristic-only, no-retraining approach can achieve.
papers.extracted_abstract: Standard speech translation cascades ASR + MT; combining into a SpeechLLM promises use of paralinguistic info and fewer cascaded errors, but existing SpeechLLMs are not truly streaming (wait for a full utterance, or emit at fixed intervals). Proposes an LLM-based architecture for real streaming S2TT where the LLM also learns to decide whether it has seen enough audio to emit a token yet, trained via automatic input-speech/output-text alignments. Across language pairs, reaches translation quality close to the non-streaming baseline at only 1-2s latency.
